extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, press/communications professionals, press agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on how to analyze, influence, and work with public opinion and the media; includes how to choose channels, frame messages, and enlist authorities to modify or conform to established beliefs. Emphasizes study of media standards, audience beliefs, and the interaction between institutions and publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the a priori judgment of the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel has to consider the a priori judgment of any public he deals with before counseling any step that would modify those things in which the public has an established belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the preexisting, often instinctive beliefs of the target public (what they already take as 'rational' or true) before proposing change; recognize many popular opinions are held without rational basis and that suspended judgment may be the only reasonable attitude for many topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attack beliefs directly; discredit authorities or create new authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is seldom effective to call names or to attempt to discredit the beliefs themselves. The counsel... must either discredit the old authorities or create new authorities by making articulate a mass opinion against the old belief or in favor of the new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid name-calling or denouncing a public's beliefs. Instead focus on undermining the credibility of the sources that sustain the belief or build and publicize new authoritative voices and organized opinion to legitimize the new position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze institutions that shape public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many outside forces that influence public opinion: parental influence, the school room, the press, motion pictures, advertising, magazines, lectures, the church, the radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map which institutions (press, schools, churches, advertising, motion pictures, radio, etc.) most influence your target public and evaluate their relative powers and constraints before planning outreach or messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing channels appropriate to the point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: In view then of the possibility of a malleable public opinion the counsel... simply utilizes existent channels to obtain expression for the point of view he represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the media and platforms (daily press, lectures, motion pictures, radio, churches, advertisements) that already reach and resonate with the intended audience rather than attempting to invent wholly new channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform to a medium's standards of newsworthiness ('fit to print')
rubrics_metrics.description: What news is 'fit to print'? By what standard is the editorial decision reached which includes one kind of news and excludes another kind? 'News' is anything timely which is significant to newspaper readers in their relations to the community, the state and the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor releases and pitches to editorial criteria: timeliness, significance to the paper's readership/community/state/nation. Use editorial judgment examples (e.g., Beecher trial) to decide whether content is defensible as newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect decency and individual rights of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The only important limitations to completeness are those imposed by the commonly accepted ideas of decency embodied in the words, 'All the news that's fit to print' and by the rights of privacy. Carefully edited newspapers discriminate between what the public is entitled to know and what an individual has a right to keep private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding what to publicize, weigh public interest against decency norms and privacy rights; expect editors to withhold material that violates those standards even if it is factual or sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messaging to public tastes and moral limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper must adapt its pleading to its clients' moral limitation... Neither may like the job, but both must face it to gain the larger end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust tone, content, and framing to the prevailing moral sensibilities and tastes of the paper's readers/audience. A message that clashes with audience mores will often be suppressed or reframed by intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of commercial constraints and advertiser/audience segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective barrier between the public and the event exists in the powerful influence which... is exerted in certain cases on the press by the so-called quality public which the newspapers' advertisers wish to reach... much of what may be attributed to censorship... is actually inadequate presentation of the events it seeks to describe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize newspapers and media may self-censor or shape coverage to serve advertisers and target demographics ('quality public'). Factor commercial incentives and audience segmentation into media selection and message framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist established points of view and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of any force which attempts to modify public opinion depends upon the success with which it is able to enlist established points of view... The moulder of public opinion must enlist the established point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek endorsement, sponsorship, or visible involvement from respected institutions and figures (e.g., prominent directors, public notables) to lend credibility and reassure the public about an organization's motives and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allied groups and leaders to legitimize controversial messages
rubrics_metrics.description: The producers... allowed group leaders and groups interested in education to come to the support of Brieux's drama and, in a sense, to sponsor the production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When handling sensitive or controversial topics, mobilize sympathetic civic groups, educators, or opinion leaders to sponsor or publicly support the message rather than attempting frontal public education from the organization's own voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor interaction and feedback; use trial balloons and sentiment monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials pointed out that the best way to insure public coöperation was to take the public into its confidence... public statements were used by the diplomats themselves as a happy means of testing popular opinion upon the various projects offered in council... each delegation maintained clipping bureaus... which gave the delegates accurate information as to the state of mind at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use test statements, 'trial balloons', press monitoring, clipping services, and other research tools to gauge public reaction and adjust strategy. Treat public relations as an iterative, feedback-driven process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select topics that are timely and significant to the readers' civic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: News is anything timely which is significant to newspaper readers in their relations to the community, the state and the nation. Who is to determine what is significant and what is not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize story angles and releases that connect to readers' immediate civic, community, or national concerns; demonstrate relevance to audience relations to amplify editorial interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be persistent and campaign consistently to change entrenched opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: A most graphic illustration of what such mediums can do to change opinions... is the woman suffrage question and its victory... The Safety First movement... The Rockefeller Foundation... brought about a change in the habits of large sections of rural populations by analysis, investigation, applied medical principles, and public education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan long-term, multi-channel campaigns using education, investigation, and repeated appeals; consistent, varied tactics (posters, lectures, films, laws) can gradually shift entrenched public attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance leading the public and conforming to public standards (give-and-take)
rubrics_metrics.description: The press, the lecturer, the screen and the public lead and are led by each other... The institutions which make public opinion conform to the demands of the public. The public responds to an equally large degree to these institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and manage the reciprocal relationship between institutions and publics: sometimes you must conform to existing tastes to gain access, other times you can lead opinion; strategy should be chosen based on relative influence and timing.
